descent: rappel off Friday's Folly Ledge, or continue one more 5.7 lead into the South Bowl and rappel from the summit
name: Friday's Folly
overview: A steep, very exposed climb on the Third Flatiron's vertical back side on surprisingly good holds, first done in 1950.

descent: three double-rope rappels down the line
name: Get A Life
overview: A demanding five-pitch crack line on the south side of a pillar. A loose chimney and groove leads into a corner, and the third pitch, a thin finger crack that overhangs, is the crux.

descent: walk south along the summit ridge, then drop west through the trees
name: Great Dihedral
overview: Easy, mountaineering-style outing up the big corner system on Eagle Rock's broad west-facing wall above the creek.

name: Ground Control to Major Tom
overview: A long, moderate South Rim outing that is cleaner low down than its neighbour, then borrows the Cimarron Slabs dike pitch before scrambling up to the buttress summit.

descent: downclimb north off the summit to a saddle, then go east through the woods back to the picnic grounds
name: Guide's Route
overview: A three-pitch classic: a crack taking hands and fingers, easier ground to a stance beneath the top overhangs at the southwest corner, then moves through overhangs to the top.

descent: climb down the summit tower's eastern flank, then scramble away northwest
name: Halls of Ivy
overview: An easy east-face line on the Third Pinnacle: a short slab past a tree, through the roof band, then a wide crack jammed to the top. Trident and another route join it high up.

descent: one-rope rap of about 75 ft north from the summit bolts, or downclimb west then north (easy)
name: Heavenly Journey
overview: A famous bold slab: a curved finger crack up to a bolted stance, then a long, nearly unprotected friction pitch.

name: Idiot Wind
overview: A long Turnkorner Buttress link-up mixing pieces of The Nose and Firebird: a finger crack and corner to start, runout face to shared bolts, then a long leftward traverse under the big roof and broken cracks through it.

approach: The route is on Old Ironsides Slab. It climbs the left side of the arch in the middle of the slab, left of the large triangular flake, on bolted belays.
descent: Rappel down the line into the gully on the right of the routes. A continuing line up dihedrals reaches the summit of the slab, but that finish means walking all the way around to get back to packs.
name: Excitable Boy
overview: Sustained face and friction climbing with long runouts. A mantle-style move about 15 ft past the last bolt on pitch 2 is the crux.

descent: rap off the cabled anchors at the summit's east end
name: Ivory Coast
overview: A right-slanting crack in a corner on Elephant Rock's east face, ending with hard jams through a strange roof.

descent: walk off east and loop around north, or abseil west from the tree located midway between the two summits
name: Monster of Rock
overview: Takes the left-hand crack of a pair of wide cracks, pushing through a roof.

descent: downclimb north off the summit to a saddle, then go east through the woods back to the picnic grounds
name: Jaws
overview: Jams, chimney moves and face holds up the right edge of River Arch, around its left side to a ledge, past bathtub-like scoops and up a short hand crack to the top.

name: Journey Home
overview: An eight-pitch outing on the sunny, airy east side of North Chasm View, reached farther down Cruise Gully past a huge boulder; the opening pitch is known to be dicey.

name: Lauren's Arete
overview: A long, sharp ridge forming the west side of SOB Gully, climbed on cracks and corners along the crest or just off it; mostly sound rock with reasonable route finding.

name: Leisure Climb
overview: One of the Black's better moderate lines, following a clean crack-and-corner system up the east side of North Chasm View with mostly adequate gear; several easier sections near the top are unprotected.

descent: This is a short crack in one of the small cliff bands below the east face, not a line to the summit. Build an anchor in a horizontal crack high on the slabs above the crack, then walk off from there and rejoin the trail around the east side of the peak.
name: Detour Crack
overview: A short, splitter crack in good rock, noticed while descending Solo Flight. It sits on one of several small cliff bands underneath the east face of Lone Eagle Peak. An anchor can be built in a crack running sideways, high on the slabs above, and from there it is possible to walk off. No one seems to

descent: rap the line with four double-rope rappels
name: Long Dong Wall (aka Bell Tower)
overview: Classic multi-pitch tower route: a crack and face start, a series of chimneys through the see-through Belfry, and wild bridging up the final slot.

descent: walk off left from the long ledge after pitch two, or rap from the summit
name: Magical Chrome Plated Semi-Automatic Enema Syringe
overview: A mega-classic moderate: a hand crack and hand traverse to a clean right-facing corner, then ramps and cracks to the summit block.

name: Medicine Man
overview: Steep, exposed four-pitch crack line up Sentinel Spire's sheer southeast face; first done with aid in 1986 and freed later.

approach: Start from the Fourth of July trailhead and hike the Arapaho Pass trail to Lake Dorothy at the pass. The route is on an unnamed peak just north of Mount Neva, rising west of the lake out of a snowfield. Go around the south side of the lake to the toe of that peak, then climb the snowfield to the rig
descent: From the top, walk and scramble to the flat summit area then find the ledge on the right-hand side marked by two upright pointed rocks. Bolted rappel anchors there lead down to a ledge with dark rock and a second set of anchors, and another rappel reaches the snowfield; two ropes are needed. Alterna
name: Peace is for the Valleys, War is for the Mountains
Musical Partners
overview: A seven-pitch outing up the leftmost crack line on the higher eastern wall, from the gully bottom to the rim. Pitch two is a long, continuous finger-to-hand crack of high quality.

name: Napa Valley
overview: A four-pitch crack route that jams its way up the cliff's highest section, starting well above and left of where a big pillar meets the ground.

descent: downclimb the south side from the summit
name: New Era
overview: Well-loved line up the big, obvious corner, done in two or three pitches; the hardest move is a layback shortly before the top belay.

descent: rap 100 ft west from the summit eyebolts, 60 m rope or doubles
name: North Arete
overview: A beginner favourite following the notched northern skyline of the First Flatiron: a roof taken on its left, a step with a well-known quartz knob, and fine views of the Divide and the city.

approach: Leave the car at the Willow Lake trailhead in the town of Crestone and follow the South Crestone trail up to just before the large open meadow, where the trail switchbacks around a big buried boulder. Look left (north) to the group of towers: on the far left is a face of polished conglomerate with a
descent: Scramble north down into the notch that joins the tower to the hillside; the step off the summit and the final step into the saddle are low fifth class, where a belay from a partner is reasonable. From the saddle, descend the gully on the west side, wrapping back around the tower to the start.
name: Nobody's Fault but My Own
overview: Four pitches. P1 (5.10, 115'): many options to reach the ledgy pod below the splitter; the right side was used. Go straight up from the grassy ledge rather than traversing left into the corner, then stay right to just under an overhang. A tight crack with finger pods (crux) leads to a traverse left

approach: The usual approach is from the Long's Peak trailhead on the east side, off Highway 7, going up the Loft and around Clark's Arrow, which is hard to find. The Great White Tower, on which the Great Chimney lies, is the tallest of the Palisade towers and takes centre stage among them. The first pitch st
descent: Walk off the Great White Tower and down the Loft; no rappel is needed. The alternative from the Palisades is to rappel into the Notch at the top of the Notch Couloir.
name: The Great Chimney
overview: A chimney slicing the northern aspect of Great White Tower, immediately left of its northwest arete, and the oldest recorded line there.

approach: Hike from the Wild Basin trailhead past the west shore of Thunder Lake, then turn north to Falcon Lake, which lies right below the peak. The route is on the west flank, where the mountain reaches the divide. Find the small buttress on the lower right of the peak, set apart by a small gully on either
descent: From the top, hike down to Boulder-Grand Pass, keeping left of the snowfield (facing downhill) to pick up the trail to the Lake of Many Winds, then return to Falcon Lake.
name: Sandwich Cannon
overview: Pilot Mountain's western side, deep in RMNP, climbing to the divide. Expect route-finding problems. Mostly loose rock, with sparse gear and anchors that are only solidly OK; runouts of 50+ feet over moderate ground are common. Fourteen pitches, mostly 5.2 to 5.7+ with 2nd and 3rd Class connections.

descent: downclimb the line, or rap northwest off the small summit
name: Point of Honor
overview: A steep little face climb on a 40 ft spire just east of Slot Rock's summit.
parent: Woodstone, Half & Half, and Slot Rock

approach: From Grand Lake, the North Inlet trail passes Lake Nokoni and ends at Lake Nanita, with the Ptarmigan Towers as its scenic backdrop; counting from the right, they run from one to five. This line is on Tower 4, starting right under the huge roof splitter that sits high on the wall. An orange pillar l
descent: From the top, scramble to the summit and then south over the saddle with Tower 5, and descend the gully on the south side behind Tower 5, bearing right when in doubt. A steep third-class grassy meadow leads back to the base. It is also possible to rappel from the top of the roof pitch down the PK li
name: Ptarmigan Reality AKA Night Moose
overview: Takes a 40 foot roof splitter 400 feet up Tower 4. Starting on PK is recommended over the original start, which is right of PK and meets it atop P2. Grades: 5.10-, 5.11, 5.6, 5.11a, 5.12+ (the roof crack, mostly hand and fist size), 5.9, 5.10, 5.8; one P2 option is 5.9 PG-13. While you belay the sec

approach: From Grand Lake, the North Inlet trail passes Lake Nokoni and ends at Lake Nanita, with the Ptarmigan Towers as its scenic backdrop; counting from the right, they run from one to five. Unoriginal Sin climbs the southeast face of Tower 2, starting in a shallow right-facing dihedral just left of the m
descent: Scramble down west from the summit on fourth-class ground, then back north to the trail.
name: Unoriginal Sin
overview: Tower 2, on its southeast-facing wall; a straightforward line up the center with good climbing and mostly good rock. An old Star Drive, ancient, and a worn bail/tat anchor suggest an earlier party. Pitch 1 is 5.10, 25m. Pitch 2 is 5.11c, 35m, past the Star Drive, belay under the roof. Pitch 3 is 5.1

name: Rotten Teeth
overview: The longest route on Big Rock, a runout journey up the northern buttress mixing a thin crack, a left-facing corner and long friction slabs.

name: Russian Arete
overview: A long arete climb following the crack system on the prow just west of SOB Gully's base: eight sustained pitches of corners and double cracks, then easier ground to the top.

descent: downclimb the chimney that splits the summit, squeeze west through the narrow slot, follow a ledge north to easy ground and walk down the north side
name: Satan's Slab
overview: A long, classic and thinly protected friction route up the smooth east face of Ridge Two, and a large roof passed on its left high up.

descent: downclimb north off the summit to a saddle, then go east through the woods back to the picnic grounds
name: Schooldaze
overview: Lieback and fist-jam a wide crack to the River Arch's western tip, then follow scoops to join Jaws for the finish.

descent: rap 165 ft with two ropes, or finish over a short hand crack to the summit
name: Shake 'n' Bake

approach: Start at the Glacier Gorge trailhead and walk toward Loch Vale. At the Andrews Glacier junction, which is easy to miss, keep low in the valley beside the glacial runoff rather than following the trail up toward the glacier; that lower line avoids the worst of the boulders on the way to the Gash. Hik
descent: From the summit, cairns lead down a small gully to the southeast to bolted rappel anchors. A few rappels reach the top of the Gash, with a class 3 downclimb after the last one, and the Gash takes you down to the trail.
name: Northeast Ridge

descent: downclimb Northwest Corner, or rap 75 ft northwest from the summit eyebolt
name: Siberian North Face

approach: Park near Sleeping Elephant Campground in the Poudre Canyon, cross the river, avoid the private property, and walk up the talus to the base of the wall. There are no trails, and the crossing is part of the route's character. The route climbs the northeast face and begins with a short bolted approach
descent: Rappel the route from its bolted belay stations, or walk off to the climber's left or right. A left walk-off follows a drainage toward the talus, or you can hike over the summit and descend the next drainage to the south. The approach talus is awkward going down.
name: Raspberry Tarts
overview: Mixed route of three pitches and beyond, rated 5.11-, on Sleeping Elephant Mountain's northeast face, reached by an arduous approach with three water crossings. Approach pitch (15m, one bolt, 5.7): avoid falling. P1: 35m, 5.10+, five bolts and some gear, with a flake to sling; keep thinner hand-size

descent: rap 21 m (70 ft) from the NW corner; or descend the summit's south crest to a gap, then step down ledges heading NW
name: South Ridge

descent: rap off the cabled anchors at the summit's east end
name: South Side Classic
overview: The old standard up Elephant Rock: a thin crack with a fixed pin to a large south-face ledge, then the southeast corner past another pin to the top.

approach: Park in the pullout along Mount Blue Sky Road and go down the gully, then follow the Abyss Lake trail south-southwest toward the wall's base. Looking northwest from the stretch between Helms Lake and Lake Fork, the wall is hard to miss; no maintained path leaves the trail for the base, so tread ligh
descent: The fourth pitch is low fifth-class ground to the ridge crest below the summit. To get off, walk to climber's right along obvious grassy ledges, with perhaps a fourth-class move or two.
name: Coming of Age
overview: Passes just left of the crux roof on Right of Passage. P1 (5.7, 140'): start in Right of Passage's chimney (5.6, loose), step left onto the face roughly 2/3 up, and climb slightly runout face to a ledge. P2 (5.10c, 115'): easy ground to an alcove, then a twin crack system with a well-protected crux;

name: Southern Arete
overview: A huge, wandering line of roughly 25 pitches up the arete that bounds the Painted Wall on its left: cracks and chimneys on the narrow lower buttress, then a steep headwall higher up.

descent: commonly downclimbed as the way off the summit
name: Southwest Face
overview: The short back-side route up the First Flatiron, slanting left with the rock layers into a little bowl with a steel eyebolt and finishing up the summit tower's west flank; it doubles as the usual downclimb.

name: Stoned Oven
overview: A long, committing line up the southern wall where the difficulty barely lets up.

descent: rap 21 m (70 ft) from the NW corner; or descend the summit's south crest to a gap, then step down ledges heading NW
name: Sunshine Daydream

descent: rap 21 m (70 ft) from the NW corner; or descend the summit's south crest to a gap, then step down ledges heading NW
name: Sunshine Face

approach: This is the mountaineer's route up T3 in the Block Tops. Reach the T3 and T4 saddle by way of T4, rappelling off the west end of T4's summit ridge, then cross the rotten catwalk in the saddle and scramble up solid blocks to a platform below the east face. The route is at the northeast corner: from t
descent: Heading on to T2 means walking to the summit ridge's west end and rappelling from boulders to the scree. Going back to the T3-T4 saddle instead uses a rappel from the bolted anchor high on the east face.
name: Northeast Corner
overview: Cross the rotten catwalk in the saddle between T4 and T3, scramble solid blocks to the east face, and look right for two big tan blocks with a notch on top under an arete that angles. First (Class 2 X, crux): traverse down and north along the wall's foot over awful orange rock, escaping right toward

approach: The route can be reached from the Spanish Creek, Willow Lakes or South Colony Lakes trailheads. The Spanish Creek approach crosses private monastery land and needs a permit arranged ahead. The Prow is the fin on the southwest ridge of Kit Carson Mountain, of Crestone conglomerate. Scramble third cla
descent: Head east a long way, going over another peak, to the wide valley in the saddle separating Kit Carson from Ellingwood, which allows a return to camp. Cutting back early leads onto steep slabs.
name: The Prow (Kit Carson)
overview: A knob-style classic on Kit Carson's south ridge. The hardest move comes at once, over a serious roof at the foot; the next two leads (5.6) sidestep a bulge, staying right of the crest, and everything above is mellower.

approach: Follow any Sneffels north face approach, then continue southwest up the drainage to the cluster of pinnacles at its head. To avoid talus, scramble up a rock buttress on the right (west) to an orange ledge below the east side of Number One, that gives access to the pinnacles' north side and The Hand.
descent: Reverse the route, or rappel from a slung block into the grassy gully northwest of the south summit, then a second rappel drops into the south gully that runs between The Hand and The Penguin. The broad gully separating those two pinnacles also serves as a way down.
name: North Arete

approach: Leave the car at the overlook near mile 16 of the Pikes Peak Highway, cross the low wall and walk down the drainage keeping the formation to your right. Work low, then climb back up to the foot of the route, using the slabby rib that guards the base of the formation. The route is on the north-northe
descent: Top out the formation, then walk south along the summit crest toward the road, keeping to the west side until grassy ledges let you step down into the drainage again. Some routes on the formation have a non-permanent rappel line.
name: Butterfingers
overview: P1: 5.10c, 120'. A ramp leads to two corners where a chockstone is slung, then roofs split by a fist crack. Save both #4s for the roofs; belay soon after the 2nd. An optional #5 suits the crack on the left below the roof. P2: 5.9, 70'. Arcing finger crack, arete used early; commit, reach easier grou

name: The Nose
overview: A classic, very exposed line straight up the rounded prow of Turnkorner Buttress, mixing a strenuous pillar crack, a layback flake and airy face climbing beside the huge ceilings.

name: The Scenic Cruise
overview: A variant of The Cruise that sidesteps its infamous offwidth pitch, trading it for a thin, devious traverse on pitch three before rejoining the parent route to the rim.

approach: Leave the car at the lot by the sixteenth highway marker and walk east to the ridge's high point. Locate the gash in the south side and The Blade. Hiking down the Dinosaur Couloir and scrambling up to the base is possible, but rappelling in has less effect on the terrain and the sheep; the anchors a
descent: Rappelling is the preferred way down, rather than hiking the Dinosaur Couloir, because it does less damage to the ground and the wildlife. The rappel anchors are behind the top-out. Tie knots in the rope ends, since the line may be longer than one rope reaches, then scramble down the gully to the ba
name: Katana Ridge
overview: Short approach, ample ledges and anchor cracks, and a really exciting arete, especially on top. Cruxes are brief and well protected. Start at the lot at mile 16 and walk east to the ridge's high point; spot The Blade from the gash on the south side. Rappelling in beats the Dinosaur Couloir for wildl

descent: rap 21 m (70 ft) from the NW corner; or descend the summit's south crest to a gap, then step down ledges heading NW
name: Tim's Solo

approach: The towers sit on the south side of the interstate in the canyon between Frisco and Copper Mountain. Reach them by taking the bike path from Copper toward Frisco, leaving the bikes after a few miles and hiking the gully directly below the towers. Tower 2 is just uphill from Tower 1. Follow the avala
descent: From the summit, rappel down the slab to the climber's left of the arete to the big ledge system, then rappel the lower two pitches of the climb to the ground.
name: Giants vs. Dragons

descent: rap off the cabled anchors at the summit's east end
name: Trunk Line
overview: A shallow crack system beside the southeast-corner roof that joins South Side Classic to the summit.

approach: Eldar Tower stands north of the upper alpine lake, reached by hiking west past Freya Tower from the Rock Creek trailhead on the east side of the Gore Range. Walk to the southeast corner of the peak, where a clean first pitch marks the start; easier, grungier variations exist on the south side.
descent: From the summit, follow fourth-class ground and a ledge system down eastward, curving round to the mountain's north side. Then locate the chute that faces south on the mountain's western flank and take it to the talus fan beneath.
name: I Found The Letters
overview: P1 (5.8, 100 ft): a clean wall, good cracks, ends at a belay ledge. P2 (5.2, 200 ft): a ledge system crossed from east to west. P3: scramble 100 ft to P4. P4 (5.9, 100 ft): one or two bouldery moves, unprotected, lead into a small corner, where gear can be placed (crux); then up and right through st

approach: The spire is in the South Rock Creek drainage, a quarter mile south of Freya Tower. Begin at the Rock Creek trailhead on the east side of the Gore Range, take the Gore Range trail south for roughly a mile, then turn southwest into the woods and follow the broad ridge to treeline. Cross the boulderfi
descent: After the short scramble to the summit, go down via the saddle on the back side of the spire and descend the second south-facing chute to the west.
name: Walk of Life
overview: Four main pitches. The first (100 ft) ascends a crack that takes hands and fists, passes a small ledge and ends at a larger ledge with an anchor. The second (150 ft) holds the crux at 5.6 and finishes on a belay ledge; a weakness to its right gives an easier variation. Then traverse 100 ft east alon

descent: from the summit's north end, follow worn ramps and ledges to a little saddle, then descend the westward gully
name: West Face
overview: An easy outing up the western flank: a slot or crack to a tree ledge, then the chimney behind that pinnacle and cracks to the top.

approach: Start at the Harrison Lake parking area, where Beehive Dome is in view. The approach is mostly bushwhacking, with a marshy creek crossing and a short scramble to the base of the dome. Go around the dome to the far left, where the slab eases to third class, and walk up it to the first summit.
descent: The route ends on the last of the traverse's summits. Return along the ridge the way you came, then turn off and drop to Harrison Lake over a small ridge. Cross the rocks by the lake and take the Harrison Lake trail back to the trailhead.
name: Beehive Five

approach: Drive to the Crags Campground and Transfer Camp at the end of the forest roads from Challis, then hike through the Frank Church Wilderness over two passes to Ship Island Lake. The Rabbit Ears Formation lies uphill to the north of camp at the lake outlet.
descent: Downclimb to the fixed anchor just under the summit and rappel from there to a big tree standing in the east gully. From then on, rappel from further big trees down that gully to the base.
name: Pace Setter

approach: Both the north and east faces are reached from Merriam Lake. Park at the end of the Forest Service road that serves the lake and follow the good trail to the lake, where there are fine camp spots. The east face is the steep wall rising directly above the lake. The route begins to the left of East Fa
descent: From the east-face summit, head north and descend the scree fields, keeping the north ridge to your right and the main summit above you on the left. Walk down and east to a small creek and follow the water back to Merriam Lake.
name: East Face – Mountaineer’s Route
overview: Grades run 5.5 to 5.7 for the most part, plus some 5.8, which depends on which line is chosen. Remote; Merriam Lake makes a beautiful camp. P1: slab, then a crack toward a roof; belay under it. P2: traverse right below the roof to a black limestone band, the best rock. Then left up a gully; rockfall

approach: The route begins on the slab at the extreme east end of the southeast face, beside the steep walls of the East Buttress. Look for the place where the green lichen climbs highest on that side of the south face.
descent: From the notch at the top of the second pitch, either scramble down the way the East Buttress is approached, or link into the East Buttress route to the summit and then come down the south slab rappels.
name: Southeast Face

approach: From the Twenty Mile Lakes trailhead north of McCall, follow the Twenty Mile Lakes trail and keep left at the fork, climbing through burnt forest and alpine meadow to the first lake. Pass the lake on its right to a ridge, follow the crest left through deadfall toward East Lake, and just short of it
descent: Rappel from the top of the last pitch, or scramble left along an exposed ramp to the summit, staying roped.
name: Pika Paradise

descent: climb on to the summit
name: Two Step
overview: The crack gives way to a chimney; skirt the overhang on its left to reach a ledge, then an overhanging crack leads to a perch under another chimney that gets you onto the summit.

area: Chimney Pond ("South") Basin - Summer Rock Routes
name: Flatiron
overview: A buttress route that tops out on the well-known Knife Edge ridge close to Baxter Peak. Most of it is sustained 5.7 and 5.8, building to a long jam crack of about 165 feet.

area: Chimney Pond ("South") Basin - Summer Rock Routes
descent: traverse southward along the ridge crest to Pamola, then drop down the Dudley Trail to the pond
name: The Armadillo
overview: The park's signature line up the tall, triangle-shaped buttress above a high basin. It is long and exposed, with plenty of low-angle scrambling plus tougher pitches ranging 5.7 through sustained 5.8 at times, varying with the line chosen; allow a long day.

approach: Drive to the Fairy Lake road, pass the Shafthouse trailhead, and park beyond the Forest Service gate beside the two well-used campsites. Pick up the narrow trail opposite the parking area, cross the creek and climb the short steep hill to the big meadow, then follow the trail nearly to the top of it
descent: Walk off. The last pitch ends on the summit of Arrowhead. Walk down the ridge west to the Bridger Ridge trail and follow it over the next rises in the ridge, not dropping too early, to a large saddle at the Sacajawea trail. Take that trail left down to the trailhead, then the road back to the parkin
name: Alpine Boogie

approach: Reach the base of the north face first by the long approach in from the Benbow Mine side. From a camp there, hike up the fresh, light-colored moraine toward the southeast to a bowl under the big east-summit face, then wrap around to the east side of the Central Rib. Start scrambling where dark rock
descent: From the west summit, drop back to the big ledge and traverse over to the east summit, which is third class with easy routefinding. Descend east, then north to northeast, onto the Mt. Wood plateau, and continue down scree and talus toward the base of the north face, keeping the distinct darker slope
name: Central Rib

approach: Follow the Gunsight Pass trail out of Lake McDonald and into the Lake Ellen Wilson basin. The central, largest buttress above the trail is Palm Springs, the second you meet coming from the west. When you draw level with it, leave the trail and climb the open beargrass slopes to the rock. The route b
descent: From the top, traverse climber's left and slightly up, and descend the first big gully on the left flank of the buttress. Follow it down until you can cross skier's right to a grassy series of ledges, cross the intermittent creek draining the basin, and work down the ledges to the talus. Steep snow
name: If I Had A Hammer
overview: Corners through stacked roofs near the buttress's southern toe. Pitches were long on 70m ropes but could be split to about 40m. Wet in places in spring and after storms. Rappelling would leave a lot of gear, as natural anchors are few. P1 (65m, 5.8): slot, corner, slab, belay near dead trees. P2 (5.

approach: From the Fairy Lake trailhead, head for Sacajawea Peak. In the bowl between Hardscrabble Peak and Sacajawea, find the obvious slab at the foot of the peak, which is the start.
descent: Above the climbing, continue along the ridge between the Airplane bowl and the Sacajawea bowl to the summit, then walk down the regular hiking trail.
name: Sacajawea direct.
overview: The opening slab is the crux: easy climbing on good rock, but nowhere to fall. The rib or gully above is easier, and its exposure is not dangerous. The slab tilts at roughly 55 degrees, the rib/gully roughly 45. It has always been done as a rope-free solo or scramble. Once the climbing ends, keep go

approach: Follow the Spirit Mountain approach to Moon Lake. From the south end of the lake, skirt the east shore and aim for the snow at the foot of the arete, then climb the steep permanent snowfield, which steepens to about 50 degrees near its top, to the base of the rock.
descent: Descend by the South Ridge, which is longer than the alternative. The South Slopes route is shorter but can hold alpine ice in the snowfield and has very loose fourth-class terrain beside it.
name: Lunar Arete

approach: Park at the East Rosebud Creek bridge below the towers, then scramble the steep gully that separates Innocence from Incubus. Start from a ledge beneath two opposing dihedrals at the bottom of Incubus. The lower tier can be bypassed by continuing up the gully to the big midway terrace.
descent: A bolted rappel station sits roughly 30 feet below the summit, reached from a tree. Long rappels from there reach the big midway ledge, and from that terrace you walk off.
name: By Many or By Few aka West Face of the Tower of Incubus

approach: From the West Fork trailhead take the trail that passes right under the formation, which is north of the trail. Leave the trail and follow ridges and gullies through forest and meadow up the slope; granitic slabs appear in the upper section, but the path only walks beneath them. Go up the gully bene
descent: Rappel to the ledge under the summit block and downclimb into the gully; climb the gully a way, then cut left into the forest. Traverse in the forest to a big clean face next to a flowered meadow, and follow the base of the Witchtowers slabs back to your packs.
name: Hocus Pocus
overview: Eight pitches. P1 5.6/5.4R, 55m, slab to an overlap belay. P2 5.8, 30m, tricky gear, easiest line to a left-facing corner and horn belay. P3 5.9, 35m, tunnel beneath the chalkstone, trend left at the roof. P4 5.10-, 35m, up the corner and past two roofs to a gear anchor. P5 5.9, 45m, crack left of t

approach: Start from the rescue cache on the floor of Tuckerman Ravine and bushwhack across, keeping the Remi Bourdage memorial boulder on your left. Work over the boulder field to the clear gully left of Lion's Head (as you face it) and follow it up to the height of a small gendarme-shaped feature. A short b
descent: The route ends just below the summit of Lion's Head. From there walk down the Lion's Head Trail, which is the trail you are standing on.
name: Lion's Head Standard

descent: scramble to the summit, then walk down the marked hiking trail
name: Endeavor
overview: A fun, long moderate on good rock, mixing corners, face moves and a hand crack up the middle of the cliff.

descent: rappel the line twice with one rope, or scramble to the summit and hike down
name: The White Streak
overview: A long varied outing that wanders up flakes, corners and a chimney before finishing on the clean white streak high on the cliff.

descent: from the summit head left to the east-side rappel anchors and enter the descent gully; bring two ropes and expect lots of downclimbing
name: Left Eyebrow
overview: A long, moderate climb to the summit with widely spaced protection and plenty of navigation decisions, so plan for a full day.

approach: The Mummy is a granite pinnacle low in Mummy Canyon, near where the canyon opens into Pinnacle Valley beneath the southwest ridge of the Needle. From the North Crest Trail take the Chimney Canyon Trail from the junction just north of the radio towers, go down its switchbacks through the limestone ba
descent: Rappel down the south face along the line of ascent, from the anchors on the summit of the pinnacle.
name: Route 1
overview: Single-pitch aid line up the south side of the spire, bulging just below the top.

descent: hike up to the crest from the summit
name: Bombs Away

approach: The ridge starts at the second Sandia tram tower. Reach it by the West Ridge trail, or by Domingo Baca Canyon, which is also the better way to the east side of the peak.
descent: From the summit, contour the slopes north of Whiskey Peak, dropping gradually to about 9,400 feet into the top of the forested gully just west of the Thumb. That gully leads down to the Old La Luz trail.
name: Whiskey Ridge
overview: Starts at tram tower number two, then runs north across 3rd and 4th class terrain, with a few short 5th class sections, that totals several hundred feet. Next come 5.5/5.6 pitches, three of them short, and then the logistical crux, The Complex: two downclimbing pitches, which apparently a 60m rope a

descent: Descent is long and serious. From the summit follow the third- and fourth-class west ridge down to the low point just before Parrot Beak Peak. From there, follow a steep, loose sandy goat trail down the gullies, downclimbing slabs and fourth-class grassy ledges, back into the main drainage below Lot
name: Southeast Arete

approach: Access is a flight to Qikiqtarjuaq, then a chartered boat or a sea kayak trip from there. From the coast, follow the north arm of the Coronation Glacier up. The line starts where rock emerges from the ice on the glacier's north margin.
descent: The way down from the top follows the rim of the canyon west and northwest, then descends into the upper end of the obvious river valley toward a tributary glacier. Where that glacier meets the main glacier there is an impassable canyon, so the line returns uphill and handrails the cliff west of the
name: Escape from Azkaban

approach: Access is a flight to Qikiqtarjuaq, then a chartered boat or a sea kayak trip from there. The route climbs the prominent ridge and buttress on the north side of the Coronation Glacier, just downstream of the split between its north and south arms. The approach begins at the bottom of the low ridge l
descent: From the top head north across the summit plateau, then trend down and to the left over wide talus and slab fields above a cliff band. A fourth-class chimney leads down through the cliff band, and from there the route exits back right out of the river valley onto the Coronation Glacier.
name: The Salami Exchange Commission
overview: The biggest route of the expedition: four tiers of steep climbing divided by easy ground, 3rd class to low 5th. Rock quality swings a lot, though most cruxes take protection well. An adventure with a little spice. The first ascent used no bolts.

name: Centerfold
overview: Follows one crack line up the face onto the summit of Perception Tower, then carries on to the highest point of Mescalito.

name: Community Pillar
overview: Begins in a wide chimney blocked by a giant chockstone, which you tunnel behind before a dihedral opening leftward, then keeps to that fissure line up the pillar through chimneys, a hole, and offwidth or hand-and-fist options.

descent: three rappels on two ropes
name: Dark Shadows
overview: Considered one of the finest 5.8 climbs in the region and once something of a soap opera. It starts up a ramp to a dark corner, then a clean corner, a lovely stemming dihedral, and a curving crack beneath a giant roof; every pitch has a good ledge for belaying.

name: Deep Space
overview: Two easy pitches lead to a deep, wide chimney that gives the route its name; stemming and a jam crack climb it, followed by delicate face climbing to a shelf below an offwidth, then more crack climbing and easier pitches to the summit.

descent: several rappels, the first a 165 ft drop from the summit bolts down to the bushy terrace above pitch 3, then a scramble to a gully
name: Geronimo
overview: A popular, good-quality route in five pitches: a bent crack to a big boulder-strewn ledge, a thin crack and face above, a black face aimed at a dihedral up on the skyline, and a gentler face finishing at the summit.

descent: scramble down the gully left of the formation with 5 half-rope rappels
name: Magic Triangle
overview: Cracks low on the left side lead to bushes, then a long fourth-class pitch crosses about 150 ft rightward along the central pale band to a crack just right of center, followed straight up. Higher come a roof at 5.9, a devious zigzag pitch and a final run to the summit.

name: Midsummer Night Scheme
overview: Climbs a broad crack that begins with scrambling and slowly steepens in difficulty, mixing fourth and fifth class; the wall is big and complicated, yet progress is quick.

name: Negro Blanco
overview: A huge right-opening chimney and corner system whose base forms a cave, marking the western edge of the dark varnished wall.

descent: rappel the route
name: Orange Clonus
overview: A long, many-pitch line on the lower southeast spur of Bridge Mountain's east peak, passing under a little dark pinnacle. A black right-facing corner opens the climb (offwidth, then fingers and hands), the middle is easy face and scrambling, and a sustained overhanging finger-to-hand crack comes lat

name: Spectrum
overview: Among the most eye-catching lines in Red Rocks, with every kind of terrain: face, flake, overhang, offwidth, chimney, corner, roof and cracks. The only thing missing is good protection.

descent: use two ropes and abseil from the paired bolts partway up pitch 4
name: The Big Horn
overview: Climbs the initial corner, then shifts over to the curving dihedral and follows it up to a roof; sidling over to the east provides entry to the roof crack, which holds the crux. Higher, a fine fissure in dark rock and some easier pitches gain the top; some stretches are poorly protected.

descent: rap in stages from the summit boulder anchors via the top-of-pitch-2 anchor to the ground; or walk off left from the higher ledge
name: The Friar

descent: doubled-rope rappel off a bolted boulder just east of the top
name: Astro Monkey

approach: Get onto the Black Lake Trail from Anthony Lake Campground or the Elkhorn Crest trailhead. A little past Lilypad Lake, take the gently rolling ski and bike trail south, then pick a path up the forested slope to the boulder field under Gunsight Dome. Gunsight Slab is directly above: work right along
descent: There are two ways down. One is a single-rope rappel from a tree on climber's right, as low on the slab as can be reached. The other is a walk-off to climber's left along the summit rocks until they end at trees, then sharply left onto the ledges that lead back down to the foot of the climb; the top
name: Zig-Zag
overview: One of several lines on a lovely slab, starting mid-ledge in the trees below it; the start has variations. P1 (5.6, 25 m) wanders over uneven ground, ending at a large flake bearing a small elderberry on its left; protection is sparse, but the flake takes a good anchor. P2 (5.7, 50 m) wanders: climb

descent: doubled-rope rappel off a bolted boulder just east of the top
name: Northwest Passage (Free)

approach: From the Hautes-Gorges park gate, take the shuttle or ride a bike to the Draveur visitor centre. Cross the bridge over the dam on foot, turn left on a hiking trail and follow it a few minutes. When a small island appears in the Malbaie River, cut straight into the woods toward the gully and climb th
descent: Descend by rappelling from trees to the right of the route. A short optional hike leads to the trailless summit of the mountain.
name: La Félix-Antoine

descent: one-rope rappel using the mahogany at the summit
name: Boomerang
overview: Pitch one's slanting finger crack is superb and fierce; pitch two is lengthy and awkward to protect.

approach: Head for the steep flank over the Strawberry Traverse, under the pale gray north-face slab that holds the start of On the Fly. Turn the corner just right of the huge solitary tree; the base is in a shaded alcove above a large healthy tree, facing the Needles Lodge.
descent: The route ends on the top of the peak. Walk off from the summit.
name: Lone Tree
overview: The line is the right-facing dihedral that stands out most on the face. Begin in an alcove in shade above the large tree. Probably climbed before. One pitch (5.7, 70 m): get past an awkward bulge at the start, then good cracks reach the summit. Walk off.

descent: After the second pitch, a short stretch of broken third-class ground leads to the summit ridge. Parties can walk west off the top, or rappel the line.
name: On The Fly
overview: Takes the longest face and slab section of the quartzite northeast face on DeMoisy Peak. P1 (5.8, 30 m): the good quartzite is bleached whitish gray; climb an arete, passing faint overlaps, then reach a crack for hands trending left, and continue on nice edges left and up to a ledge belay. P2 (5.10a

descent: rappel off the summit
name: Jagged Edge

descent: single rappel off a tree at the summit
name: Plumb Line
overview: Striking crack splitting a steep, textured wall, running from tips width to thin hands. You walk right beneath it en route to the big buttress, so it is hard to miss.

descent: route-finding descent down the east then south sides of the summit: three rappels (roughly 100, 65 and 85 ft), gully and slab walking between
name: The Standard Thumb
overview: The long easy classic of the cliff: nine pitches linking a corner, chimneys, a hand crack under a roof, a deep awkward trough and a final summit block. Ledges and bushes break it up, and a variation skirts the dirtiest gully pitches.

approach: Leave the car at the Bald Mountain trailhead and hike the Notch Mountain trail up to Notch Lake. Swing north around the lake, then push northwest through the trees to a talus field, which leads to the foot of the buttress's east side. The route is the direct line up the middle of the buttress; once
descent: Rappel from the anchor at the summit down to the midway ledge, take off the rope, and scramble climber's left over class II-III ground toward The Notch. Reach a gully running perpendicular to the notch, work down it until a ledge system on its right side doglegs right into the notch, then go down th
name: European Death Notch

approach: Leave the car at the Bald Mountain trailhead and hike the Notch Mountain trail up to Notch Lake. Swing north around the lake, then push northwest through the trees to a talus field, which leads to the foot of the buttress's east side. The route follows European Death Notch to its roof, then breaks l
descent: Rappel from the anchor at the summit down to the midway ledge, take off the rope, and scramble climber's left over class II-III ground toward The Notch. Reach a gully running perpendicular to the notch, work down it until a ledge system on its right side doglegs right into the notch, then go down th
name: Juggernotch Arete

approach: Leave the car at the Bald Mountain trailhead and hike the Notch Mountain trail up to Notch Lake. Swing north around the lake, then push northwest through the trees to a talus field, which leads to the foot of the buttress's east side. The route was the first on the buttress; once on top of the talus
descent: Rappel from the anchor at the summit down to the midway ledge, take off the rope, and scramble climber's left over class II-III ground toward The Notch. Reach a gully running perpendicular to the notch, work down it until a ledge system on its right side doglegs right into the notch, then go down th
name: Notch yer Average Corner

descent: rappel off the summit
name: Wave Break
overview: A blade of stone shaped like a cresting wave; its steep, leaning eastern side is climbed on questionable gear.

descent: single rappel using two ropes off summit anchors
name: West Face
overview: A two-pitch route up the western flank of a small spire in a remote setting. A powdery chimney and a good finger crack lead to a ledge, then an old bolt ladder goes up the north ridge to a runout easy finish. The ladder can be freed or aided.

name: Apex Buttress
overview: Seven pitches, climbing the buttress that stands out on the left of Tungsten Lake.
